title: Diomedes as a river in flood
intro: After one last miniature death scene, the narrative singles out Diomedes. A sustained flood simile makes his force almost impossible to contain; Pandarus then appears to stop it with an arrow. The page ends in the middle of his boast.

notes.text: ἀρητήρ is a praying priest, here of the river Scamander. ἐτέτυκτο is pluperfect middle/passive of τεύχω, with the developed sense ‘was constituted / served as.’ The relative clause describes Dolopion, the father. θεὸς δ᾽ ὣς means ‘like a god’; ὥς follows its comparison word. τίετο is imperfect passive of τίω, ‘was honoured,’ with δήμῳ referring to the community.

The repeated τόν resumes Hypsenor after the family digression. μεταδρομάδην is an adverb, ‘running after him, in pursuit.’ ἀΐξας is aorist participle of ἀΐσσω, ‘dart’; ἔλασε is aorist of ἐλαύνω, here ‘struck.’ φασγάνῳ is instrumental dative, ‘with a sword,’ and ὦμον marks the part hit.

ἔξεσε is aorist of ξέω, ‘scrape, cut’; ἀπό supplies the severing, ‘cut off.’ χείρ can include the arm, not only the hand. πέσε is unaugmented second aorist of πίπτω. ὄσσε is accusative dual, ‘the two eyes,’ with κατά. πορφύρεος gives death a dark, surging colour; μοῖρα κραταιή is ‘overpowering fate.’

γνοίης is second singular root-aorist optative of γιγνώσκω, from γνω-. With ἄν it means ‘you could not tell.’ ποτέροισι introduces the indirect question ‘with which side’; μετείη is optative of μέτειμι in the sense ‘be among,’ not ‘go after.’ ὁμιλέοι is uncontracted present optative of ὁμιλέω, ‘mingle / fight among.’

ἠέ and ἦ introduce the alternatives ‘whether … or.’ The point is Diomedes’ rapid movement through the fighting, not uncertainty about his allegiance. θῦνε is imperfect of θύνω, ‘rush, rage.’ ἄμ is an assimilated form of ἀνά before π in πεδίον, ‘across the plain.’

ἐοικώς is perfect active participle of ἔοικα, with present meaning ‘resembling,’ and takes the dative. πλήθοντι, present participle of πλήθω, describes a swollen river; χειμάρρῳ means winter-torrent-like, fed by seasonal rains. Keep ποταμῷ, πλήθοντι, and χειμάρρῳ together across the line break.

γέφυραι here are barriers or embankments across water; ‘bridges’ can mislead if imagined as modern road bridges. ἐεργμέναι is perfect passive participle of ἔργω, ‘enclose, bar,’ describing their constructed barrier function. ἰσχανόωσιν is an epic expanded present form of ἰσχανάω, ‘hold back.’ ἕρκεα, ‘enclosures,’ is neuter plural with singular ἴσχει.

ἀλωάων is uncontracted genitive plural of ἀλωή, ‘cultivated plot / orchard’; ἐριθηλέων means ‘luxuriant.’ ἐπιβρίσῃ is aorist subjunctive of ἐπιβρίθω, ‘weigh heavily, press down,’ in the generalizing ὅτε clause. Διὸς ὄμβρος is Zeus’ rain. αἰζηῶν means vigorous men; their ἔργα are the cultivated works or labour the flood destroys.

κατήριπε is second aorist of κατερείπω, ‘fell in ruins’; the singular can take neuter plural ἔργα as subject. The matching ὑπό phrases connect flood and warrior as destructive forces. πυκιναὶ φάλαγγες are close-packed battle formations, without requiring the later technical hoplite phalanx. πολέες περ ἐόντες is concessive, ‘although they were many.’

Lycaon’s son is Pandarus, introduced here by patronymic. ἐνόησε is aorist of νοέω, ‘noticed’; θύνοντα and κλονέοντα both describe Diomedes. ἐτιταίνετο is imperfect middle of τιταίνω, ‘stretch,’ here drawing his bow. τόξα is a conventional plural for the bow; καμπύλα describes its curvature.

τυχών is second-aorist participle of τυγχάνω, ‘hitting the mark.’ θώρηκος γύαλον denotes the curved plate of the breastplate, specifying where the arrow strikes near the shoulder. ἔπτατο is aorist middle of πέτομαι, ‘flew’; πικρός, literally ‘sharp / bitter,’ characterizes the arrow’s painful force.

διέσχε is second aorist of διέχω, ‘went right through’; παλάσσετο, imperfect middle/passive of παλάσσω, describes the armour being spattered with blood. βέβληται is perfect middle/passive of βάλλω, ‘has been hit,’ the result on which Pandarus bases his boast. ὄρνυσθε is a second-plural middle imperative, ‘rise / charge!’ κέντορες ἵππων means ‘drivers of horses.’
